cards.q: During the early part of the sinoatrial node pacemaker potential, which ion moves into the cell through the funny channels?
cards.a: Na+.
options: Na+
K+
Ca2+
Cl-
cards.explanation: The funny current is a slow inward Na+ current through HCN channels, and it starts the drift away from the most negative point of the cycle back toward threshold. K+ moves out of a pacemaker cell during repolarization, so it cannot be the ion driving the membrane in the depolarizing direction. Ca2+ entry is real but comes later in the pacemaker potential, first through T-type and then through L-type channels. Cl- movement plays no part in the sinoatrial pacemaker sequence.

cards.q: What opens the funny channels of a sinoatrial node cell?
cards.a: Hyperpolarization after the last action potential.
options: Depolarization of the membrane to about -40 mV
Hyperpolarization after the last action potential
Ca2+ binding to the channel from inside the cell
Stretch of the nodal cell membrane during filling
cards.explanation: HCN channels are called funny because hyperpolarization opens them, the opposite of most voltage-gated channels, so the current switches on exactly when the cell is most negative near -60 mV. Depolarization to about -40 mV is threshold, which opens the L-type Ca2+ channels for the upstroke, not the funny channels. These channels are gated by voltage and tuned by cyclic AMP, not opened by intracellular Ca2+ binding, and they are not mechanically gated by stretch.

cards.q: Which channels carry the final part of the pacemaker drift up to threshold, just before the L-type channels open?
cards.a: T-type Ca2+ channels.
options: Fast voltage-gated Na+ channels
Delayed rectifier K+ channels
T-type Ca2+ channels
ATP-sensitive K+ channels
cards.explanation: Once the funny current has brought the membrane part of the way up, transient (T-type) Ca2+ channels open and carry Ca2+ inward for the last stretch to threshold near -40 mV. Fast Na+ channels are essentially absent in nodal tissue and would be inactivated at these voltages anyway, which is why the nodal upstroke is slow. Delayed rectifier K+ channels carry the repolarizing current after the peak, and ATP-sensitive K+ channels open during metabolic stress rather than in the normal pacemaker cycle.

cards.q: Which ion movement produces the upstroke of the sinoatrial node action potential?
cards.a: Ca2+ moving in through L-type channels.
options: K+ moving out of the cell
Na+ moving in through fast voltage-gated channels
Cl- moving into the cell
Ca2+ moving in through L-type channels
cards.explanation: At threshold the L-type Ca2+ channels open and Ca2+ influx carries the upstroke, which is why the nodal action potential rises far more slowly than a ventricular one. Fast Na+ channels carry the upstroke in ventricular contractile cells, not in the node, and this is the single contrast most often collapsed. K+ efflux repolarizes the cell after the peak and moves the membrane in the opposite direction. Cl- currents are not part of the nodal action potential.

cards.q: What repolarizes a sinoatrial node cell after the peak of its action potential?
cards.a: K+ moving out of the cell.
options: K+ moving out of the cell
Na+ pumped out by the Na+/K+ ATPase
Ca2+ carried out by the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger
Cl- moving out of the cell
cards.explanation: Repolarization is K+ efflux through delayed rectifier K+ channels while the L-type Ca2+ channels close, the same ion and the same direction that repolarize every excitable cell you have studied. The Na+/K+ ATPase does export Na+, but it moves far too little charge per second to repolarize an action potential and it runs continuously rather than in a burst. The Na+/Ca2+ exchanger clears Ca2+ from the cytosol over many milliseconds and actually carries net positive charge inward, so it is depolarizing. Cl- efflux is not a feature of nodal repolarization.

cards.q: Roughly what membrane potential must a sinoatrial node cell reach before it fires an action potential?
cards.a: About -40 mV.
options: About -90 mV
About -70 mV
About -40 mV
About 0 mV
cards.explanation: Threshold in the sinoatrial node is near -40 mV, the voltage at which enough L-type Ca2+ channels open to make the upstroke self-sustaining. About -90 mV is the stable resting potential of a ventricular contractile cell, which is a resting value and not a threshold. About -70 mV is the resting potential typical of a neuron. Zero mV is above the peak of the nodal action potential, so the cell would already have fired long before reaching it.

cards.q: What is the intrinsic firing rate of the sinoatrial node in an isolated heart with no autonomic input?
cards.a: About 100 beats per minute.
options: About 30 beats per minute
About 50 beats per minute
About 100 beats per minute
About 160 beats per minute
cards.explanation: Stripped of nerves, sinoatrial tissue depolarizes to threshold about 100 times a minute. A resting heart rate near 70 is lower than that because vagal tone continuously slows the node, so the resting rate is the intrinsic rate minus parasympathetic braking. About 50 per minute matches the atrioventricular node and about 30 matches Purkinje fibers, the slower backup pacemakers. About 160 is a rate the heart reaches only with strong sympathetic drive, not on its own.

cards.q: Why does the sinoatrial node, rather than the atrioventricular node, normally set heart rate?
cards.a: Its pacemaker cells reach threshold faster than any other pacemaker tissue.
options: It is the only cardiac tissue capable of spontaneous depolarization
Its pacemaker cells reach threshold faster than any other pacemaker tissue
It is the only tissue that receives sympathetic innervation
It has the most negative threshold, so it needs the smallest stimulus
cards.explanation: Several regions can depolarize spontaneously, but the fastest one wins: the sinoatrial node reaches threshold first and its impulse depolarizes the slower pacemakers before they ever get there on their own. The atrioventricular node and Purkinje fibers also have unstable membrane potentials, so the node is not unique in that ability, only in its speed. Both nodes receive sympathetic and parasympathetic innervation. Threshold is roughly similar across pacemaker tissues; it is the steepness of the drift, not the threshold value, that decides which one leads.

cards.q: Norepinephrine binds beta-1 receptors on sinoatrial node cells and raises cyclic AMP. What happens to the pacemaker potential?
cards.a: The slope becomes steeper, so threshold is reached sooner.
options: The slope becomes steeper, so threshold is reached sooner
The slope becomes shallower, so threshold is reached later
Threshold shifts to a more negative value with no change in slope
The maximum diastolic potential becomes more negative
cards.explanation: Cyclic AMP binds the HCN channels directly and increases the funny current, and it also increases Ca2+ entry, so the drift toward threshold is faster and the interval between beats is shorter. A shallower slope is exactly what parasympathetic stimulation produces, so that option describes the opposite arm of the autonomic nervous system. Sympathetic stimulation works mainly by changing the rate of drift, not by relocating threshold. A more negative maximum diastolic potential is also a parasympathetic effect, since it comes from opening K+ channels.

cards.q: Vagal release of acetylcholine opens K+ channels in sinoatrial node cells. Predict the effect on the maximum diastolic potential and on heart rate.
cards.a: A more negative maximum diastolic potential and a slower rate.
options: A less negative maximum diastolic potential and a faster rate
No change in maximum diastolic potential and a slower rate
A more negative maximum diastolic potential and a slower rate
A more negative maximum diastolic potential and a faster rate
cards.explanation: Opening K+ channels lets more K+ leave, driving the membrane closer to the K+ equilibrium potential, so the cell starts each drift from a more negative point and has further to travel to threshold. Extra distance plus a reduced funny current means a longer interval between beats and a slower heart rate. A more negative starting point cannot speed the cell up, so the option pairing hyperpolarization with a faster rate has the logic backwards. A less negative maximum diastolic potential with a faster rate describes what sympathetic stimulation does, not acetylcholine.

cards.q: A drug blocks L-type Ca2+ channels in the sinoatrial node. What happens to the upstroke of the nodal action potential?
cards.a: It becomes slower and smaller, because that current is reduced.
options: It is unchanged, because the nodal upstroke is carried by Na+
It becomes slower and smaller, because that current is reduced
It becomes faster, because fast Na+ channels take over the job
It is replaced by a maintained plateau at the threshold voltage
cards.explanation: The nodal upstroke is Ca2+ influx through L-type channels, so blocking those channels directly reduces the current that produces it and both the rate of rise and the peak fall. The option claiming no change assumes a Na+ upstroke, which is true for ventricular contractile cells but not for nodal cells. Fast Na+ channels cannot compensate because they are inactivated at the depolarized voltages a nodal cell lives at. A plateau requires sustained Ca2+ entry, which is exactly what the drug has removed.

cards.q: A drug shifts the threshold of sinoatrial node cells from -40 mV to -30 mV without changing the slope of the pacemaker potential or the maximum diastolic potential. What happens to heart rate?
cards.a: It falls, because the cell must drift further before it reaches threshold.
options: It rises, because the cell is now closer to zero millivolts
It is unchanged, because the slope of the drift was not altered
It rises, because less Ca2+ entry is needed to reach threshold
It falls, because the cell must drift further before it reaches threshold
cards.explanation: Firing rate is set by how long the drift takes, which depends on both the slope and the distance to be covered. Raising threshold from -40 to -30 mV adds 10 mV to that distance, so at unchanged slope each cycle takes longer and rate falls. The slope being unchanged does not protect the rate, because time to threshold is distance divided by slope. Being closer to zero is not an advantage; the cell has to reach threshold from below, and a higher threshold is further away.

cards.q: The sinoatrial node stops firing entirely. Which tissue is most likely to take over, and at roughly what rate?
cards.a: The atrioventricular node, at 40 to 60 per minute.
options: Purkinje fibers, at about 60 to 100 beats per minute
Ordinary atrial muscle, at about 70 beats per minute
The atrioventricular node, at 40 to 60 per minute
The bundle branches, at about 90 beats per minute
cards.explanation: The next fastest pacemaker takes over, and that is the atrioventricular junction, whose cells drift to threshold about 40 to 60 times a minute. Purkinje fibers can also pace, but far more slowly, at roughly 20 to 40 per minute, so the rate given in that option belongs to the sinoatrial node. Ordinary atrial and ventricular muscle have stable resting potentials and no funny current, so they cannot generate their own rhythm. Bundle branch tissue is part of the same slow His and Purkinje escape system and does not pace at 90.

cards.q: Why does the sinoatrial node action potential rise far more slowly than a ventricular action potential?
cards.a: The upstroke uses L-type Ca2+ channels, which pass current more slowly.
options: Nodal cells have a much larger diameter, so charge spreads more slowly through them
Nodal cells are hyperpolarized, so they start further away from threshold
Nodal cells contain more Na+/K+ ATPase working against the upstroke current
The upstroke uses L-type Ca2+ channels, which pass current more slowly
cards.explanation: Speed of an upstroke is set by the channel that carries it, and L-type Ca2+ channels have slower gating and smaller currents than the fast voltage-gated Na+ channels that drive the ventricular upstroke. Nodal cells are in fact relatively depolarized, near -60 mV rather than -90 mV, which is why their fast Na+ channels sit inactivated and unavailable. Nodal cells are small, not large, and cell size affects conduction along tissue rather than the rate of rise in a single cell. Pump activity is far too small a current to slow an upstroke.

cards.q: Which of these changes in a sinoatrial node cell would raise heart rate?
cards.a: A steeper pacemaker potential.
options: A more negative maximum diastolic potential
A steeper pacemaker potential
A threshold shifted toward zero
A longer nodal action potential
cards.explanation: Rate is the inverse of the time from one upstroke to the next, and a steeper drift covers the distance to threshold in less time, so beats come closer together. A more negative maximum diastolic potential lengthens the distance the drift has to cover and slows the rate. A threshold shifted toward zero also lengthens that distance and slows the rate. A longer action potential adds time to each cycle before the drift can even begin, which slows the rate as well.

cards.q: A transplanted heart has no autonomic innervation. At rest its rate is close to 100 beats per minute, while a healthy person with the same fitness rests near 70. What accounts for the difference?
cards.a: The transplanted node runs at its intrinsic rate because the vagal braking normally present is absent.
options: The transplanted node runs at its intrinsic rate because the vagal braking normally present is absent
The transplanted node has lost its sympathetic supply, and sympathetic withdrawal raises the rate
Denervation makes the pacemaker potential steeper by opening more L-type Ca2+ channels
Denervation raises threshold in the nodal cells, which shortens each cycle
cards.explanation: The intrinsic rate of the sinoatrial node is about 100 per minute, and a resting rate of 70 is the product of continuous vagal tone slowing that intrinsic rhythm. Remove the nerves and the brake goes with them, so the node reverts to its own pace. Losing sympathetic input would tend to lower rate rather than raise it, so sympathetic withdrawal cannot explain a faster heart. Denervation removes signals rather than adding L-type channels, and raising threshold would lengthen each cycle and slow the heart.

cards.q: A compound selectively blocks the funny current in the sinoatrial node. Trace the consequences in order.
cards.a: Shallower pacemaker slope, longer time to threshold, lower heart rate.
options: Steeper pacemaker slope, shorter time to threshold, higher heart rate
Shallower pacemaker slope, longer time to threshold, lower heart rate
Shallower pacemaker slope, longer time to threshold, unchanged heart rate
Unchanged pacemaker slope, longer action potential, lower heart rate
cards.explanation: The funny current is the inward Na+ current that starts the drift, so removing it makes the early pacemaker potential shallower, the cell needs longer to climb from about -60 mV to threshold near -40 mV, and fewer beats fit into a minute. A steeper slope would follow from adding funny current, as sympathetic stimulation does, not from blocking it. Rate cannot stay unchanged when the time between upstrokes lengthens, since rate is simply the inverse of cycle length. The action potential itself is carried by Ca2+ and K+ currents and is not lengthened by an HCN blocker.

cards.q: Surgery destroys the sinoatrial node, and the atrioventricular junction takes over, pacing the heart at about 45 beats per minute. Why is the escape rate lower than the sinoatrial rate it replaced?
cards.a: Atrioventricular pacemaker cells have a shallower pacemaker potential, so they take longer to reach threshold.
options: Atrioventricular pacemaker cells cannot depolarize spontaneously and must wait for atrial stretch
Atrioventricular pacemaker cells have a shallower pacemaker potential, so they take longer to reach threshold
Atrioventricular cells repolarize to a less negative potential, which delays the next upstroke
Atrioventricular cells lack L-type Ca2+ channels, so each upstroke fails several times before succeeding
cards.explanation: Every pacemaker tissue in the heart drifts spontaneously, but they do it at different speeds, and the junctional cells have the shallower drift, so each cycle takes longer and the escape rhythm is slower. They do not need stretch or any external trigger; that is what makes them a functioning escape pacemaker at all. Repolarizing to a less negative potential would shorten the distance to threshold and speed the cell up, which is the opposite of what is seen. L-type Ca2+ channels are present and carry the junctional upstroke, otherwise there would be no escape rhythm.

cards.q: A sinoatrial node cell fires at 60 beats per minute. Each cycle is an action potential lasting 300 ms plus a pacemaker potential lasting 700 ms. Sympathetic stimulation steepens the drift so the pacemaker potential now takes 200 ms, with no change in action potential duration. What is the new rate?
cards.a: About 120 beats per minute.
options: About 86 beats per minute
About 100 beats per minute
About 120 beats per minute
About 200 beats per minute
cards.explanation: The new cycle length is 300 ms plus 200 ms, which is 500 ms, and 60 seconds divided by 0.5 seconds per beat gives 120 beats per minute. About 200 comes from timing only the action potential and forgetting that the drift still occupies 200 ms of every cycle. About 86 comes from using the old 700 ms drift alone. About 100 would require a 600 ms cycle, which is what you get if you shorten the action potential instead of the pacemaker potential.

cards.q: What is the resting membrane potential of a ventricular contractile cell during phase 4?
cards.a: About -90 mV.
options: About -90 mV
About -70 mV
About -60 mV
About -40 mV
cards.explanation: A ventricular contractile cell rests near -90 mV, held there by inward rectifier K+ channels that keep the membrane close to the K+ equilibrium potential, and unlike a nodal cell it stays there until an impulse arrives. About -70 mV is the resting value of a typical neuron. About -60 mV is the most negative point a sinoatrial node cell reaches, and it does not stay there because the funny current immediately starts the drift. About -40 mV is nodal threshold, not a resting potential.

cards.q: Which ion movement produces phase 0, the rapid upstroke of the ventricular action potential?
cards.a: Na+ moving in through fast voltage-gated channels.
options: Ca2+ moving in through L-type channels
Na+ moving in through fast voltage-gated channels
K+ moving out through delayed rectifier channels
Na+ moving in through HCN funny channels
cards.explanation: Fast voltage-gated Na+ channels open in a fraction of a millisecond and let Na+ rush down its electrochemical gradient, which is why the ventricular upstroke is steep and the cell can conduct quickly to its neighbors. L-type Ca2+ entry does happen, but it sustains the plateau and is the upstroke current in the sinoatrial node rather than in a contractile cell. K+ efflux moves the membrane in the repolarizing direction, the opposite of an upstroke. HCN channels belong to pacemaker tissue and are not part of the contractile cell action potential.

cards.q: What produces phase 1, the small dip immediately after the peak of the ventricular action potential?
cards.a: Fast Na+ channels inactivate as a K+ current flows out.
options: L-type Ca2+ channels close briefly and then open again
Cl- floods into the cell through open leak channels
Fast Na+ channels inactivate as a K+ current flows out
The Na+/K+ ATPase briefly runs in the reverse direction
cards.explanation: Phase 1 is a brief notch: the fast Na+ channels inactivate so the inward current stops, and at the same moment a transient outward K+ current carries positive charge out, dropping the membrane slightly before the plateau holds it. L-type Ca2+ channels are opening during this window, not closing and reopening. Cl- influx is not a significant current in the human ventricular action potential. The Na+/K+ ATPase runs steadily in one direction and moves far too little charge to cause a visible notch.

cards.q: Which two ion movements balance each other during phase 2, the plateau of the ventricular action potential?
cards.a: Ca2+ entering through L-type channels and K+ leaving through K+ channels.
options: Na+ entering through fast channels and K+ leaving through K+ channels
Ca2+ entering through L-type channels and Cl- entering through Cl- channels
Ca2+ entering through L-type channels and K+ leaving through K+ channels
Na+ entering through HCN channels and Ca2+ leaving through the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger
cards.explanation: The plateau exists because slow inward Ca2+ current through L-type channels nearly cancels the outward K+ current, so net charge movement is close to zero and the membrane hangs near 0 mV for roughly 200 ms. Fast Na+ channels are already inactivated by this point, so they contribute nothing to the plateau. Cl- entry is not a meaningful plateau current. HCN channels are pacemaker channels and are absent from contractile cells.

cards.q: Which ion movement produces phase 3, repolarization of the ventricular cell?
cards.a: K+ moving out of the cell.
options: Ca2+ moving out of the cell through L-type channels
Na+ moving out of the cell through fast channels
Cl- moving into the cell
K+ moving out of the cell
cards.explanation: Phase 3 begins when the L-type Ca2+ channels finish closing while delayed rectifier K+ channels stay open, so the outward K+ current is no longer balanced and the membrane falls back toward -90 mV. Voltage-gated channels carry ions down their gradients, so Ca2+ and Na+ channels can only let those ions in, never out. Cl- influx is not the repolarizing current of cardiac muscle.

cards.q: What holds the ventricular cell membrane at its resting potential during phase 4?
cards.a: Open K+ leak channels holding the membrane near -90 mV.
options: A steady inward funny current balanced against Ca2+ entry
Open K+ leak channels holding the membrane near -90 mV
Continuous Cl- entry that holds the membrane negative
Fast Na+ channels held slightly open at a low steady level
cards.explanation: Between beats the dominant conductance is K+ through inward rectifier leak channels, so the membrane sits close to the K+ equilibrium potential near -90 mV and stays stable until the next impulse arrives. A funny current is what makes nodal phase 4 unstable, and contractile cells do not have one, which is exactly why they do not pace themselves. Cl- distribution is close to equilibrium at rest and does not set the resting potential in cardiac muscle. Fast Na+ channels are closed at rest, not partly open.

cards.q: How long does a ventricular action potential last, compared with a skeletal muscle action potential?
cards.a: About 250 ms, compared with about 2 ms.
options: About 25 ms, compared with about 2 ms
About 250 ms, compared with about 2 ms
About 250 ms, compared with about 100 ms
About 1000 ms, compared with about 2 ms
cards.explanation: A ventricular action potential runs roughly 200 to 300 ms because of the plateau, while a skeletal muscle fiber finishes its action potential in a couple of milliseconds. That hundredfold difference is the whole reason cardiac muscle cannot be summed into tetanus. About 100 ms is closer to the length of a skeletal muscle twitch, which is the contraction, not the action potential. A full second would be longer than an entire cardiac cycle at a resting heart rate.

cards.q: Which phase gives the ventricular action potential its unusually long duration?
cards.a: Phase 2, the plateau.
options: Phase 0, the upstroke
Phase 1, the notch
Phase 2, the plateau
Phase 4, the resting potential
cards.explanation: The plateau holds the membrane depolarized for about 200 ms because inward Ca2+ current offsets outward K+ current, and that single phase accounts for nearly the whole duration of the action potential. The upstroke is over in a millisecond or two, and the notch is briefer still. Phase 4 is the interval between action potentials rather than a part of one, and its length changes with heart rate.

cards.q: A toxin blocks fast voltage-gated Na+ channels in ventricular muscle. Predict the effect on phase 0.
cards.a: The upstroke becomes slower and smaller, because less Na+ current flows.
options: The upstroke becomes slower and smaller, because less Na+ current flows
The upstroke becomes faster because K+ efflux is unopposed
The upstroke is unchanged because Ca2+ carries it
The upstroke reverses and becomes a hyperpolarization
cards.explanation: Phase 0 is Na+ influx through fast channels, so blocking them reduces the inward current available and the membrane rises more slowly and to a lower peak, which also slows conduction to neighboring cells. K+ efflux opposes depolarization, so removing an inward current cannot make the upstroke faster. Assuming Ca2+ carries the upstroke confuses the contractile cell with the sinoatrial node. A blocked channel simply passes less current; it does not drive the membrane in the opposite direction.

cards.q: A drug blocks L-type Ca2+ channels in ventricular muscle. What happens to the action potential?
cards.a: The plateau shortens, so the action potential is briefer.
options: The upstroke slows, but the overall duration is unchanged
The plateau shortens, so the action potential is briefer
The plateau lengthens, because K+ efflux is also reduced
The resting potential becomes less negative than before
cards.explanation: The plateau is held up by inward Ca2+ current, so with less of it the outward K+ current wins sooner, repolarization starts earlier, and total action potential duration falls. The upstroke is a Na+ event and is not affected by an L-type blocker. Blocking Ca2+ channels does nothing to K+ channels, so there is no reason for the plateau to lengthen. Resting potential is set by K+ leak conductance and is not shifted by a Ca2+ channel blocker.

cards.q: A drug blocks the delayed rectifier K+ channels of ventricular muscle. Predict the effect on the action potential.
cards.a: Repolarization is slowed, so the action potential lasts longer.
options: Repolarization is slowed, so the action potential lasts longer
Repolarization is faster, so the action potential is shorter
The upstroke is slowed, so the peak is lower
The resting potential becomes more negative
cards.explanation: Phase 3 depends on outward K+ current, so reducing it means the membrane takes longer to fall back to -90 mV and the action potential, along with the QT interval on an ECG, is prolonged. Blocking a repolarizing current cannot speed repolarization up. The upstroke is a Na+ event, so its rate of rise is untouched. Less K+ conductance moves the resting membrane away from the K+ equilibrium potential, making it less negative rather than more.

cards.q: During the plateau of the ventricular action potential, the membrane potential barely changes for about 200 ms. What does that tell you about the currents?
cards.a: Inward Ca2+ current and outward K+ current are nearly equal.
options: All voltage-gated channels are closed, so no current is flowing at all
Inward Ca2+ current and outward K+ current are nearly equal
The Na+/K+ ATPase is holding the membrane voltage constant
Membrane resistance has fallen to zero, so the voltage cannot change
cards.explanation: A flat voltage does not mean no current; it means the inward and outward currents cancel, and in the plateau that balance is Ca2+ entering through L-type channels against K+ leaving through K+ channels. If all channels were shut, the membrane would return to its resting potential rather than sitting near 0 mV. The Na+/K+ ATPase moves too little charge per second to clamp the voltage. Zero resistance would mean the membrane could not hold any potential at all, including the resting potential.

cards.q: Why does a ventricular action potential last about a hundred times longer than a skeletal muscle action potential?
cards.a: Sustained Ca2+ entry holds the membrane depolarized in a plateau.
options: Cardiac cells are much larger, so it takes longer to move enough charge
Sustained Ca2+ entry holds the membrane depolarized in a plateau
Cardiac cells lack a Na+/K+ ATPase to restore the gradients quickly
Cardiac K+ channels open faster, which drags out repolarization
cards.explanation: The plateau is the difference: skeletal muscle repolarizes as soon as its Na+ channels inactivate, while cardiac muscle keeps an inward Ca2+ current running that opposes repolarization for roughly 200 ms. Cell size does not set action potential duration; single channels and their kinetics do, and cardiac cells are in fact smaller than skeletal fibers. Cardiac cells have plenty of Na+/K+ ATPase, and in any case the pump restores gradients over minutes rather than shaping a single action potential. Faster K+ channel opening would shorten repolarization, not lengthen it.

cards.q: Extracellular K+ rises from 4 to 7 mEq/L. Which way does the resting membrane potential of a ventricular cell move?
cards.a: It becomes less negative, moving toward threshold.
options: It becomes more negative, moving away from threshold
It becomes less negative, moving toward threshold
It does not change, because the Na+/K+ ATPase compensates immediately
It becomes more negative, because more K+ leaves the cell
cards.explanation: Resting potential tracks the K+ equilibrium potential, and raising extracellular K+ reduces the gradient driving K+ out, so the equilibrium potential and the resting potential both shift toward zero. Less negative means closer to threshold, which is why moderate hyperkalemia first makes cardiac cells more excitable before inactivating Na+ channels and making them less excitable. A smaller outward gradient cannot drive more K+ out, so the option reasoning from increased efflux has the gradient backwards. The pump adjusts over minutes and cannot hold the membrane potential fixed against an acute change.

cards.q: A ventricular cell is artificially held at -60 mV instead of -90 mV and then stimulated. What happens to the upstroke?
cards.a: It is smaller, because many fast Na+ channels are inactivated.
options: It is larger, because the cell starts out much closer to threshold
It is unchanged, because threshold is a fixed voltage value
It is smaller, because many fast Na+ channels are inactivated
It is faster, because less Na+ influx is needed to fire
cards.explanation: Fast Na+ channels inactivate when a cell sits depolarized, and they only recover once the membrane returns near -90 mV, so at -60 mV a large share of them are unavailable and the upstroke that follows is weak and slow. Starting closer to threshold makes the cell easier to trigger but does not give it more Na+ current to work with, so amplitude falls rather than rises. Threshold voltage is not the issue; availability of channels is. A weaker inward current always produces a slower rate of rise, never a faster one.

cards.q: A drug reduces Ca2+ entry through L-type channels in ventricular muscle by half. Trace the consequences through to contraction.
cards.a: Smaller plateau Ca2+ current, less Ca2+ released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, weaker contraction.
options: Smaller plateau Ca2+ current, less Ca2+ released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, weaker contraction
Smaller plateau Ca2+ current, more Ca2+ released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, unchanged contraction
Smaller plateau Ca2+ current, slower upstroke, weaker contraction
Larger K+ current, longer plateau, stronger contraction
cards.explanation: The Ca2+ that enters during the plateau is the trigger for calcium induced calcium release, so halving it means the ryanodine receptors release less stored Ca2+, less Ca2+ reaches troponin, and the contraction is weaker. Release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum follows the trigger, so it cannot increase when the trigger falls. The upstroke belongs to fast Na+ channels and is not affected by an L-type blocker. Blocking an inward current shortens the plateau rather than lengthening it, and weakens rather than strengthens the beat.

cards.q: A toxin prevents fast Na+ channels in ventricular muscle from inactivating, so they stay open once triggered. Predict the effect on the action potential and the refractory period.
cards.a: The action potential is prolonged and the refractory period lengthens with it.
options: The action potential is shortened and the refractory period shortens with it
The action potential is prolonged and the refractory period lengthens with it
The upstroke disappears and the cell can no longer be excited
The plateau disappears but the total duration is unchanged
cards.explanation: Inactivation of the Na+ channels is what ends phase 0 and allows the notch and eventually repolarization, so if the channels stay open the inward current persists, the membrane is held depolarized far longer, and the action potential drags on. Because the refractory period lasts until the membrane repolarizes enough for Na+ channels to reset, it lengthens along with the action potential. The upstroke is not lost, since the channels still open normally; it is the switching off that fails. Losing inactivation adds inward current, which cannot shorten the action potential or abolish the plateau.

cards.q: A recording from a ventricular cell shows a normal upstroke and normal resting potential, but the membrane stays near 0 mV for 500 ms instead of 200 ms before repolarizing. Which change best explains the tracing?
cards.a: Outward K+ current during the plateau is reduced.
options: Fast Na+ channels are opening more slowly
Outward K+ current during the plateau is reduced
The resting K+ leak conductance is increased
The Na+/K+ ATPase has been blocked
cards.explanation: The plateau length is set by the balance between inward Ca2+ current and outward K+ current, so if K+ efflux is reduced the balance tips inward, repolarization is delayed, and the plateau stretches. Slower Na+ channel opening would change the upstroke, which the tracing says is normal. More resting K+ conductance would make the resting potential more negative and would speed repolarization, not delay it. Blocking the pump raises intracellular Na+ over minutes and does not directly hold a single plateau open.

cards.q: Both a sinoatrial node cell and a ventricular contractile cell are isolated in a dish with no stimulation. The nodal cell keeps firing and the ventricular cell stays silent. Which two differences explain this?
cards.a: The ventricular cell lacks a funny current and its K+ conductance holds phase 4 stable.
options: The ventricular cell lacks a funny current and its K+ conductance holds phase 4 stable
The ventricular cell lacks L-type Ca2+ channels and cannot generate an upstroke on its own
The ventricular cell has a lower threshold and so inactivates itself before firing
The ventricular cell lacks a Na+/K+ ATPase, so its gradients run down and it cannot fire
cards.explanation: Automaticity needs two things a contractile cell does not have: an inward current that starts at negative voltages, which is the funny current through HCN channels, and an unstable phase 4, which is impossible when inward rectifier K+ channels clamp the membrane near the K+ equilibrium potential. The ventricular cell has plenty of L-type Ca2+ channels; they run the plateau and would fire fine if the cell ever reached threshold. A lower threshold would make a cell easier to excite, not silent. Removing the pump would eventually stop the cell entirely rather than explain a quiet but excitable cell.

cards.q: Where does a normal cardiac impulse begin?
cards.a: In the sinoatrial node, high in the wall of the right atrium.
options: In the sinoatrial node, high in the wall of the right atrium
In the atrioventricular node, in the floor of the right atrium
In the bundle of His, at the top of the interventricular septum
In the left atrium, near where the pulmonary veins enter
cards.explanation: The sinoatrial node sits high in the right atrial wall next to the superior vena cava, and because its cells drift to threshold fastest, that is where each normal beat starts. The atrioventricular node is downstream, in the floor of the right atrium near the tricuspid valve, and only paces if the sinoatrial node fails. The bundle of His is further downstream still, carrying the impulse into the septum. The left atrium receives the impulse through internodal and interatrial pathways rather than generating it.

cards.q: What is the correct order of the cardiac conduction pathway?
cards.a: Sinoatrial node, internodal pathways, atrioventricular node, bundle of His, bundle branches, Purkinje fibers.
options: Sinoatrial node, atrioventricular node, internodal pathways, Purkinje fibers, bundle branches, bundle of His
Sinoatrial node, bundle of His, atrioventricular node, internodal pathways, bundle branches, Purkinje fibers
Atrioventricular node, sinoatrial node, internodal pathways, bundle of His, Purkinje fibers, bundle branches
Sinoatrial node, internodal pathways, atrioventricular node, bundle of His, bundle branches, Purkinje fibers
cards.explanation: The impulse leaves the sinoatrial node, spreads across the atria through the internodal pathways to the atrioventricular node, is delayed there, then runs down the bundle of His into the two bundle branches and finally out through the Purkinje fibers to ventricular muscle. The versions that place the bundle of His before the atrioventricular node reverse the only electrical route between atria and ventricles. Putting Purkinje fibers before the bundle branches reverses the branching order, since Purkinje fibers are the terminal twigs. The sinoatrial node always precedes the atrioventricular node in a normal beat.

cards.q: Where is the atrioventricular node located?
cards.a: In the floor of the right atrium near the tricuspid valve.
options: In the interventricular septum, just below the aortic valve
In the floor of the right atrium near the tricuspid valve
In the roof of the left atrium, next to the mitral valve
In the apex of the right ventricle, at the base of the papillary muscles
cards.explanation: The atrioventricular node lies low in the interatrial septum, in the floor of the right atrium near the tricuspid valve and coronary sinus, which places it right at the gateway between atria and ventricles where the delay is imposed. The interventricular septum carries the bundle of His and bundle branches, which are downstream of the node. The left atrium and the ventricular apex contain no nodal tissue; the apex is where Purkinje fibers first deliver the impulse to working muscle.

cards.q: How long is the atrioventricular nodal delay in a normal heart?
cards.a: About 0.1 second.
options: About 0.01 second
About 0.1 second
About 0.5 second
About 1.0 second
cards.explanation: Conduction through the atrioventricular node takes roughly 100 ms, which is most of the normal PR interval of 0.12 to 0.20 second. A delay of 0.01 second would be too brief to let the atria finish emptying. Half a second would be longer than the systole of an entire cardiac cycle at rest and would separate atrial from ventricular contraction badly. A full second is about the whole cardiac cycle at 60 beats per minute.

cards.q: Which structure is the only normal electrical connection between the atria and the ventricles?
cards.a: The bundle of His.
options: The internodal pathways
The coronary sinus
The bundle of His
The Purkinje network of the atria
cards.explanation: A ring of fibrous connective tissue insulates the atria from the ventricles, and the bundle of His is the single strand of conducting tissue that crosses it, which is why a block there can separate the two chambers completely. The internodal pathways run within the atria only, from the sinoatrial to the atrioventricular node. The coronary sinus is a vein returning blood from the heart wall and conducts nothing. Purkinje fibers are ventricular, not atrial.

cards.q: Which part of the conduction system conducts most slowly?
cards.a: The atrioventricular node.
options: The Purkinje fiber network
The bundle of His
The atrioventricular node
The bundle branches in the septum
cards.explanation: Atrioventricular nodal cells conduct at roughly 0.05 m/s, the slowest tissue in the heart, and that slowness is what creates the delay between atrial and ventricular contraction. Purkinje fibers are the fastest, at roughly 2 to 4 m/s, so the ventricles can be activated almost at once. The bundle of His and the bundle branches are also fast conducting tissue built for speed rather than delay.

cards.q: Which fibers deliver the impulse from the bundle branches to ventricular muscle?
cards.a: Purkinje fibers.
options: Internodal pathway fibers
Purkinje fibers
Chordae tendineae
Intercalated disc fibers
cards.explanation: Purkinje fibers are large, fast conducting cells that fan out from the ends of the bundle branches, beginning at the apex, and hand the impulse to working ventricular muscle. Internodal pathways carry the impulse across the atria, upstream of the atrioventricular node. Chordae tendineae are the tendinous cords anchoring the atrioventricular valve leaflets and carry no impulse. Intercalated discs are junctions between individual cardiac muscle cells, not a named conduction pathway.

cards.q: What is the purpose of the atrioventricular delay?
cards.a: It gives the atria time to finish contracting before the ventricles contract.
options: It gives the atria time to finish contracting before the ventricles contract
It allows the ventricles to repolarize fully before the next atrial beat
It lets the coronary arteries fill while the ventricles are depolarized
It prevents the sinoatrial node from firing more than 100 times per minute
cards.explanation: Holding the impulse for about 100 ms means atrial contraction is complete before ventricular contraction begins, so the ventricles receive the final portion of their filling volume rather than being squeezed shut on partly filled chambers. Ventricular repolarization is controlled by the length of the ventricular action potential and the refractory period, not by the nodal delay. Coronary filling happens mainly during ventricular relaxation, well after this delay. The nodal delay does not limit sinoatrial firing rate, which is set by the pacemaker potential.

cards.q: Why do atrioventricular nodal cells conduct so slowly?
cards.a: They are small, poorly coupled, and use a slow Ca2+ upstroke.
options: They are wrapped in myelin, which slows the impulse between the nodes
They are small, poorly coupled, and use a slow Ca2+ upstroke
They lack a Na+/K+ ATPase, so their ion gradients are shallow
They are separated by synapses that add a chemical transmission delay
cards.explanation: Three features stack up: a narrow fiber offers high internal resistance, few gap junctions mean less current passes to the next cell, and a Ca2+ driven upstroke rises slowly compared with a Na+ driven one. Cardiac tissue has no myelin at all, which is a nervous system feature. Nodal cells have normal ion pumps and normal gradients. There are no synapses inside the conduction system; cardiac cells are electrically coupled directly through gap junctions.

cards.q: If the atrioventricular delay were abolished so the impulse passed straight from atria to ventricles, what would happen to ventricular filling?
cards.a: It would fall, because the ventricles would contract while the atria are still emptying.
options: It would rise, because the two chambers would contract together and generate more pressure
It would fall, because the ventricles would contract while the atria are still emptying
It would be unchanged, because most filling is passive
It would rise, because diastole would be longer
cards.explanation: Atrial contraction tops off the ventricles at the end of diastole, so if the ventricles start contracting at the same moment the atrioventricular valves are pushed shut early and that final contribution is lost. Simultaneous contraction does not add pressure usefully; it makes the atria push against closed valves. Most filling is indeed passive, but the atrial contribution still matters, and it matters much more at high heart rates when passive filling time is short. Removing the delay shortens rather than lengthens the interval before ventricular systole.

cards.q: A person has a block in the left bundle branch. How does the left ventricle become activated?
cards.a: By slow cell to cell spread from the right ventricle, so activation takes longer.
options: It is not activated at all and does not contract
By slow cell to cell spread from the right ventricle, so activation takes longer
By a direct atrial pathway that bypasses the ventricular conduction system
By the Purkinje fibers of the left ventricle firing spontaneously in time with the right
cards.explanation: Cardiac muscle cells are joined by gap junctions, so an impulse that cannot use the left bundle still reaches the left ventricle by spreading muscle cell to muscle cell, which is much slower than Purkinje conduction and widens the QRS complex. The ventricle is not silent, it is simply activated late and less uniformly. There is no normal accessory route from atria to ventricular muscle apart from the bundle of His. Purkinje fibers can pace when nothing else reaches them, but at 20 to 40 per minute and not synchronized to the other ventricle.

cards.q: Why does ventricular contraction begin at the apex and move toward the base?
cards.a: Purkinje fibers reach the apex first, so blood is driven upward.
options: The apex has thicker muscle, so it depolarizes at a lower threshold
Purkinje fibers reach the apex first, so blood is driven upward
The atrioventricular valves open at the apex and pull the impulse down
The base is insulated by the fibrous skeleton and cannot contract
cards.explanation: The bundle branches run down the interventricular septum to the apex before the Purkinje fibers fan out, so the apex depolarizes and contracts first and the wave of contraction wrings blood upward toward the aortic and pulmonary valves. Wall thickness does not change threshold; depolarization order is set by the conduction pathway. Valve movement is a consequence of pressure changes and does not steer the impulse. The fibrous skeleton insulates the atria from the ventricles electrically, but the base of the ventricles is working muscle and contracts normally.

cards.q: Sympathetic stimulation acts on the atrioventricular node. Predict the effect on conduction through it.
cards.a: Conduction speeds up, so the delay is shorter.
options: Conduction speeds up, so the delay is shorter
Conduction slows, so the delay is longer
Conduction is blocked entirely at high rates
Conduction is unaffected, since only the sinoatrial node is innervated
cards.explanation: Sympathetic fibers increase Ca2+ current in nodal tissue, so atrioventricular cells reach threshold and pass the impulse on faster, shortening the delay and the PR interval, which is useful at high heart rates when there is less time to spare. Slowed conduction with a longer delay is the parasympathetic effect. Block at high rates is what happens with excess vagal tone or disease, not with sympathetic drive. Both nodes are richly innervated by both branches of the autonomic nervous system.

cards.q: Strong vagal stimulation reaches the atrioventricular node. What happens to the time between atrial and ventricular depolarization?
cards.a: It lengthens, because acetylcholine slows nodal conduction.
options: It shortens, because acetylcholine speeds nodal conduction
It lengthens, because acetylcholine slows nodal conduction
It is unchanged, because the vagus reaches only the sinoatrial node
It shortens, because a slower heart rate leaves more time for conduction
cards.explanation: Acetylcholine reduces Ca2+ current and increases K+ conductance in atrioventricular nodal cells, so they take longer to reach threshold and pass the impulse on, which lengthens the delay and the PR interval. Speeding conduction is a sympathetic effect. The vagus supplies the atrioventricular node as well as the sinoatrial node, which is why strong vagal activity can both slow the heart and block conduction. A slower rate does leave more time between beats, but that does not change how fast a single impulse crosses the node.

cards.q: Which step in the conduction pathway accounts for most of the flat segment between the end of the P wave and the start of the QRS complex?
cards.a: Conduction through the atrioventricular node.
options: Spread of the impulse through atrial muscle
Conduction through the atrioventricular node
Conduction through the Purkinje fibers
Repolarization of the atria
cards.explanation: The line is flat because the tissue conducting at that moment, the atrioventricular node, is too small to generate a voltage the surface electrodes can see, and its slow conduction fills most of that 100 ms. Atrial spread produces the P wave itself, which comes just before this segment. Purkinje conduction is extremely fast and occurs immediately before and during the QRS. Atrial repolarization does occur around this time but is small and buried under the QRS complex, and it does not create the delay.

cards.q: In a normal heart, atrial spread takes about 30 ms, the atrioventricular node adds about 100 ms, and the His and Purkinje system takes about 30 ms. How long after the sinoatrial node fires do the ventricles begin to depolarize, and which ECG measurement matches that time?
cards.a: About 0.16 second, matching the PR interval.
options: About 0.13 second, matching the QRS duration
About 0.16 second, matching the PR interval
About 0.16 second, matching the QT interval
About 0.30 second, matching the PR interval
cards.explanation: Adding 30 plus 100 plus 30 gives 160 ms, or 0.16 second, and that is exactly what the PR interval measures: the time from the onset of atrial depolarization to the onset of ventricular depolarization, sitting comfortably inside the normal range of 0.12 to 0.20 second. The QRS duration measures only the ventricular depolarization that follows, normally under 0.12 second. The QT interval covers ventricular depolarization plus repolarization and runs closer to 0.40 second. The 0.30 second figure double counts the nodal delay.

cards.q: An accessory pathway connects atrial muscle directly to ventricular muscle, bypassing the atrioventricular node. Predict the consequences for the PR interval and for ventricular filling.
cards.a: A shorter PR interval and reduced filling, because the ventricles fire too early.
options: A longer PR interval and reduced filling, because conduction takes an extra step
A shorter PR interval and reduced filling, because the ventricles fire too early
A shorter PR interval and improved filling, because the beat is more efficient
An unchanged PR interval, because the atrioventricular node still conducts normally
cards.explanation: The accessory route skips the only place in the heart that deliberately slows conduction, so ventricular depolarization begins early and the PR interval shortens. Losing the delay means the ventricles start contracting while the atria are still emptying, so the atrial contribution to filling is cut short and stroke volume suffers. An extra parallel route cannot lengthen the PR interval, since the impulse takes whichever path is faster. The node still conducts, but it is no longer the first to arrive, so the interval does change.

cards.q: Purkinje fibers can depolarize spontaneously at about 20 to 40 per minute, yet they never pace a healthy heart. Why not?
cards.a: The sinoatrial impulse reaches them before their own drift does.
options: They lose their pacemaker channels once the heart has matured
The sinoatrial impulse reaches them before their own drift does
The fibrous skeleton prevents any impulse they generate from spreading
Their threshold is too positive to be reached by any spontaneous drift
cards.explanation: This is overdrive suppression in its simplest form: at 70 beats per minute an impulse arrives every 850 ms or so, far sooner than a Purkinje cell needs to drift to threshold on its own, so the fast pacemaker resets the slow one on every beat. The channels are still there, which is why the fibers can pace once the sinoatrial impulse stops reaching them. The fibrous skeleton separates atria from ventricles and would not stop a ventricular impulse from spreading through ventricular muscle. Their threshold is reachable, just not quickly.

cards.q: An impulse from the sinoatrial node reaches the atria normally but never arrives at the ventricles. What does the ventricular myocardium do, and why?
cards.a: It is driven by a slow escape pacemaker in the His and Purkinje system.
options: It is driven by a slow escape pacemaker in the His and Purkinje system
It contracts at the atrial rate, because the atria and ventricles are mechanically coupled
It stops entirely, because ventricular tissue has no automaticity of any kind
It contracts at a faster rate, because the atrioventricular delay has been removed
cards.explanation: With the fast pacemaker cut off, the next tissue down the line drifts to its own threshold and takes over, giving a slow ventricular escape rhythm of roughly 20 to 40 per minute that keeps some output going. The chambers are coupled by pressure and valves, not by mechanical transmission of an impulse, so the ventricles cannot simply follow the atrial rate. Ventricular conducting tissue does have automaticity, which is precisely why the heart does not stop. Losing conduction cannot speed the ventricles up, since the impulse never gets there at all.

cards.q: What defines the absolute refractory period of a cardiac muscle cell?
cards.a: No stimulus of any strength can trigger a second action potential.
options: No stimulus of any strength can trigger a second action potential
A stronger than normal stimulus can trigger a second action potential
The cell responds normally but contracts more weakly
The cell is depolarized but cannot release Ca2+ from the sarcoplasmic reticulum
cards.explanation: During the absolute refractory period the fast Na+ channels are inactivated and cannot reopen, so the cell simply will not fire again no matter how large the stimulus. A stimulus that is strong enough to work describes the relative refractory period, which follows the absolute one. A normal response with a weaker contraction is not a refractory state at all. Ca2+ release is happening vigorously during this period, which is why the cell is contracting.

cards.q: What makes the ventricular cell absolutely refractory for so long?
cards.a: Fast Na+ channels stay inactivated until the membrane repolarizes.
options: The sarcoplasmic reticulum is empty and cannot release more Ca2+
Fast Na+ channels stay inactivated until the membrane repolarizes
The Na+/K+ ATPase has not yet restored the resting ion gradients
Acetylcholine remains bound to the membrane throughout the contraction
cards.explanation: Inactivated Na+ channels only recover when the membrane returns toward its negative resting potential, and the long plateau holds the cell depolarized for about 200 ms, so recovery is postponed for most of the contraction. The sarcoplasmic reticulum still contains Ca2+; refractoriness is a membrane property, not a store depletion problem. The Na+/K+ ATPase restores gradients slowly and continuously and a single action potential barely dents them. Acetylcholine acts on nodal tissue and does not gate the ventricular refractory period.

cards.q: Roughly how long is the refractory period of ventricular muscle?
cards.a: About 250 ms.
options: About 2 ms
About 25 ms
About 250 ms
About 1000 ms
cards.explanation: The ventricular refractory period runs about 250 ms, which is close to the length of the action potential and therefore close to the length of the contraction itself. About 2 ms is the refractory period of a skeletal muscle fiber, which is why skeletal muscle can be stimulated again long before it relaxes. About 25 ms would still leave most of the contraction unprotected. A full second is longer than the entire cardiac cycle at a resting rate.

cards.q: What happens during the relative refractory period?
cards.a: A stronger than normal stimulus can trigger an action potential.
options: The cell cannot fire again under any circumstances at all
The cell fires normally but produces no contraction at all
A stronger than normal stimulus can trigger an action potential
The cell fires spontaneously without any stimulus being applied
cards.explanation: By the relative refractory period some fast Na+ channels have recovered but many have not, so a larger stimulus can recruit enough of them to fire, and the resulting upstroke is slower and smaller than normal. Complete unresponsiveness defines the absolute refractory period that precedes it. Firing without contracting would require a failure of excitation contraction coupling, which is a separate problem. Spontaneous firing is a property of pacemaker tissue, not a refractory state.

cards.q: What is tetanus in a muscle?
cards.a: A sustained contraction from stimuli arriving faster than relaxation.
options: A sustained contraction from stimuli arriving faster than relaxation
A single maximal twitch produced by one unusually strong stimulus
A contraction that occurs without any action potential reaching the fiber
A prolonged relaxation caused by depleted Ca2+ stores in the cell
cards.explanation: Tetanus is summation taken to its limit: each new action potential adds Ca2+ before the previous release has been pumped away, so twitches fuse into one smooth maintained contraction. A single strong twitch is not tetanus no matter how large it is, because tetanus requires repeated stimulation. Contraction without an action potential does not occur in striated muscle. Depleted Ca2+ stores would weaken contraction, which is the opposite of a maintained one.

cards.q: How does the refractory period of skeletal muscle compare with the length of its own twitch?
cards.a: The refractory period is about 2 ms and the twitch about 100 ms, so restimulation is possible.
options: The refractory period is about 2 ms and the twitch about 100 ms, so restimulation is possible
The refractory period and the twitch are both about 100 ms, so restimulation is impossible
The refractory period is about 250 ms while the twitch lasts about 100 ms, so the fiber must relax first
The refractory period is about 100 ms while the twitch lasts about 2 ms, so restimulation is impossible
cards.explanation: A skeletal fiber recovers its Na+ channels within a couple of milliseconds while the mechanical twitch is still developing over 100 ms, and that mismatch is the reason skeletal muscle can summate and be tetanized. A refractory period equal to or longer than the twitch is the cardiac arrangement, which is exactly what prevents tetanus there. A 250 ms refractory period is the cardiac value, not the skeletal one. A twitch of 2 ms confuses the mechanical event with the action potential.

cards.q: Which part of the ventricular action potential does the absolute refractory period span?
cards.a: From the upstroke through most of repolarization.
options: Only the plateau phase
Only the resting period between action potentials
Only the upstroke itself
From the upstroke through most of repolarization
cards.explanation: Na+ channels inactivate at the top of the upstroke and stay inactivated as long as the membrane is depolarized, so the absolute refractory period covers phase 0, all of phase 2, and most of phase 3 until the membrane has repolarized to roughly -50 mV. Limiting it to the upstroke would leave the long plateau unprotected. Limiting it to the plateau would ignore that the cell is already unresponsive from the moment it fires. Phase 4 is when the cell is fully recovered and most excitable, which is the opposite of refractory.

cards.q: Why can cardiac muscle not be tetanized?
cards.a: Its refractory period lasts nearly as long as its own contraction.
options: It has no sarcoplasmic reticulum, so Ca2+ cannot accumulate in the cytosol
Its cells are electrically isolated from one another, so stimuli cannot spread
Its contraction is too weak for individual twitches to add together usefully
Its refractory period lasts nearly as long as its own contraction
cards.explanation: By the time a cardiac cell can be excited again, the contraction it is already producing is nearly over, so there is no window in which twitches can overlap and fuse. Cardiac twitches are perfectly strong enough to summate if they were allowed to; the block is timing, not force. Cardiac muscle has a sarcoplasmic reticulum and uses it heavily during every beat. Cardiac cells are electrically connected by gap junctions, which is what lets the impulse spread cell to cell in the first place.

cards.q: Suppose cardiac muscle could be tetanized. What would happen to pumping?
cards.a: The ventricles could not refill, so output would fall to nearly zero.
options: Output would be unchanged, because filling is driven by venous pressure
The ventricles would relax permanently and fill without any limit
Output would rise, because the ventricles would generate more force per beat
The ventricles could not refill, so output would fall to nearly zero
cards.explanation: A pump has to alternate between filling and emptying, so a maintained contraction leaves no diastole, the ventricles never refill, and after one or two beats there is nothing left to eject. Extra force is useless if the chamber is empty. Venous pressure does drive filling, but it cannot fill a chamber whose walls are locked in contraction and whose pressure exceeds venous pressure. Tetanus is sustained contraction, not sustained relaxation.

cards.q: A second stimulus is delivered to a ventricular cell 100 ms after the upstroke, during the plateau. What happens?
cards.a: Nothing, because the cell is absolutely refractory.
options: A second action potential of normal size occurs
A second action potential of reduced size occurs
Nothing, because the cell is absolutely refractory
The cell hyperpolarizes and the contraction ends early
cards.explanation: At 100 ms the cell is still in the plateau with its fast Na+ channels inactivated, so no stimulus of any size can produce another action potential. A normal sized second action potential would require full recovery, which does not happen until the cell has repolarized. A reduced action potential is possible in the relative refractory period later in phase 3, not during the plateau. A stimulus delivers depolarizing current and cannot hyperpolarize the cell.

cards.q: A stimulus is delivered to a ventricular cell 400 ms after the upstroke, once it has returned to -90 mV. What happens?
cards.a: A normal action potential and a normal separate contraction.
options: A normal action potential and a normal separate contraction
No response, because the refractory period lasts a full second
A reduced action potential, because Na+ channels are still recovering
A contraction that sums with the first one
cards.explanation: By 400 ms the action potential is over, the membrane is back at rest, and the Na+ channels have recovered, so the cell responds fully and produces an entirely separate beat. The refractory period is about 250 ms, not a full second, so the cell is no longer protected. Partial recovery describes the relative refractory period, which has already passed by 400 ms. Summation is impossible here because the first contraction has ended before the second action potential begins.

cards.q: A stimulus arrives during the relative refractory period of a ventricular cell. How does the resulting action potential compare with a normal one?
cards.a: It has a slower upstroke and a lower peak, and conducts slowly.
options: It has a faster upstroke, because the cell is already partly depolarized
It has a normal upstroke but no plateau at all
It is identical, because action potentials are all or none events
It has a slower upstroke and a lower peak, and conducts slowly
cards.explanation: Only some Na+ channels have recovered, so less inward current is available, the upstroke rises slowly to a lower peak, and because conduction speed depends on how fast each cell depolarizes its neighbor, the impulse also spreads more slowly. The all or none rule holds for a fully recovered cell; a partially recovered one gives a genuinely smaller response. Starting from a partly depolarized membrane reduces the channels available rather than adding speed. The plateau depends on L-type Ca2+ channels and is not the phase that fails here.

cards.q: A drug lengthens the ventricular plateau from 200 ms to 400 ms. Predict the effect on the refractory period and on the highest heart rate the ventricles can follow.
cards.a: A longer refractory period and a lower maximum rate.
options: A longer refractory period and a lower maximum rate
A longer refractory period and an unchanged maximum rate
A shorter refractory period and a higher maximum rate
An unchanged refractory period and a lower maximum rate
cards.explanation: The cell stays refractory until it repolarizes, so stretching the plateau stretches the refractory period with it, and beats that arrive before recovery simply cannot be conducted, which lowers the fastest rate the ventricles can sustain. The maximum rate cannot stay unchanged when the minimum interval between usable beats has grown. Lengthening the plateau cannot shorten refractoriness, since the two move together. The refractory period is not independent of action potential duration in cardiac muscle.

cards.q: Which statement correctly contrasts summation in skeletal and cardiac muscle?
cards.a: Only skeletal muscle can summate, since it recovers before its twitch ends.
options: Both can summate, but cardiac muscle needs a much stronger stimulus to do it
Neither can summate, because both recover only after the twitch is over
Only skeletal muscle can summate, since it recovers before its twitch ends
Cardiac muscle can summate, but only at rates above 150 beats per minute
cards.explanation: The deciding factor is the ratio of refractory period to contraction time: about 2 ms against 100 ms in skeletal muscle, which leaves a wide window for a second stimulus, against roughly 250 ms against 250 ms in cardiac muscle, which leaves essentially none. Stimulus strength cannot overcome an absolutely refractory membrane, so no amount of extra current lets cardiac muscle summate. Skeletal muscle clearly does summate, which is how it grades force. Fast heart rates shorten both the action potential and the refractory period together, so summation still does not occur.

cards.q: Why must the heart relax fully between beats?
cards.a: Ventricular filling happens during relaxation, so without it there is no volume to eject.
options: Ventricular filling happens during relaxation, so without it there is no volume to eject
The Na+/K+ ATPase can only work while the muscle is relaxed
The atrioventricular valves can only close while the ventricles are relaxed
Action potentials cannot be conducted while the muscle is contracting
cards.explanation: Stroke volume is limited by end diastolic volume, and the ventricles only fill when their walls are relaxed and chamber pressure is below atrial pressure, so relaxation time directly limits pump output. The Na+/K+ ATPase runs continuously and does not pause for contraction. The atrioventricular valves close at the start of contraction, not during relaxation; they open during relaxation. Cardiac impulses conduct through contracting muscle perfectly well, as the spread of each normal beat shows.

cards.q: A premature stimulus reaches ventricular muscle late in the relative refractory period. Trace what happens to that beat.
cards.a: A small, slowly rising action potential and a weaker contraction.
options: A small, slowly rising action potential and a weaker contraction
A normal action potential that produces a stronger contraction because it comes early
No action potential at all, because the cell is still absolutely refractory
A normal action potential that fuses with the previous contraction
cards.explanation: Late in phase 3 only a fraction of the fast Na+ channels have recovered, so the upstroke is small and slow, conduction from cell to cell is sluggish because each cell depolarizes its neighbor weakly, and less Ca2+ entry means a weaker beat. It cannot be normal, because normal requires full recovery. It is not silent either, since the absolute refractory period has already ended, which is what makes this window dangerous rather than safe. Fusion with the previous contraction would be summation, which the refractory period still prevents.

cards.q: At a heart rate of 200 beats per minute, how much of each cardiac cycle is left for filling if ventricular contraction and its refractory period occupy 250 ms?
cards.a: About 50 ms, which is far too little for adequate filling.
options: About 50 ms, which is far too little for adequate filling
About 150 ms, which is adequate at rest
About 300 ms, which is unchanged from resting values
About 550 ms, because the cycle lengthens at high rates
cards.explanation: At 200 beats per minute each cycle lasts 60000 divided by 200, which is 300 ms, and subtracting the 250 ms occupied by contraction leaves only about 50 ms of diastole. That collapse of filling time is why extremely fast rates reduce stroke volume and eventually cardiac output, and why the real heart shortens its action potential as rate rises. About 150 ms would require a 400 ms cycle, which is a rate of 150. About 300 ms is the whole cycle, not the part left over. Cycle length shortens as rate rises, never lengthens.

cards.q: An experimental drug shortens the ventricular refractory period to 50 ms without changing the length of the contraction. What becomes possible that normally is not?
cards.a: The cell can be re-excited while it is still contracting, so twitches could summate.
options: The cell can be re-excited while it is still contracting, so twitches could summate
The cell can generate a larger single contraction with no change in Ca2+ entry
The atrioventricular delay would lengthen to compensate
Conduction through the ventricles would stop entirely
cards.explanation: The refractory period is the only thing keeping a second action potential from arriving mid contraction, so cutting it to 50 ms opens a long window during which a new stimulus can add Ca2+ to a cytosol that has not yet been cleared, and summation and tetanus become possible. A single contraction cannot grow larger without more Ca2+ reaching troponin. The atrioventricular delay is a property of nodal conduction and does not adjust in response to ventricular refractoriness. Shortening refractoriness makes the tissue more excitable, not less, so conduction would not stop.

cards.q: Skeletal muscle grades its force by summation and recruitment, but the heart cannot use either. How does cardiac muscle change the force of a beat instead?
cards.a: By changing how much Ca2+ reaches the myofilaments and how far the fibers are stretched.
options: By changing how much Ca2+ reaches the myofilaments and how far the fibers are stretched
By recruiting additional ventricular cells that were previously silent
By lengthening the refractory period so that each beat lasts longer
By increasing the amplitude of the action potential above its all or none level
cards.explanation: Because gap junctions make the ventricle contract as one unit and the long refractory period rules out summation, cardiac force is graded within each beat, by the amount of Ca2+ delivered to troponin and by the length tension advantage of a more filled ventricle. There are no reserve cells to recruit, since every ventricular cell is depolarized on every beat. A longer refractory period limits rate rather than adding force. Action potential amplitude is all or none in a fully recovered cell and is not the variable the heart uses.

cards.q: Which electrical event does the P wave represent?
cards.a: Atrial depolarization.
options: Atrial repolarization
Depolarization of the sinoatrial node itself
Atrial contraction
Atrial depolarization
cards.explanation: The P wave is the voltage produced as depolarization sweeps across both atria, and atrial contraction follows it rather than being what the ECG records. An ECG shows electrical events only, so contraction is never what a wave represents. Atrial repolarization does happen, but it is small and hidden under the QRS complex. The sinoatrial node itself contains far too little tissue to produce a deflection at the body surface.

cards.q: Which electrical event does the QRS complex represent?
cards.a: Ventricular depolarization.
options: Ventricular repolarization
Ventricular contraction
Ventricular depolarization
Conduction through the atrioventricular node
cards.explanation: The QRS is the large deflection produced when depolarization spreads through the thick ventricular walls, and its size reflects the amount of muscle involved. Ventricular repolarization is the T wave, a slower and smaller event. Contraction is mechanical and begins shortly after the QRS, but it is not what the tracing records. Atrioventricular nodal conduction produces no visible deflection because the node is tiny; it appears as the flat segment before the QRS.

cards.q: Which electrical event does the T wave represent?
cards.a: Ventricular repolarization.
options: Atrial repolarization
Ventricular relaxation
Ventricular repolarization
The plateau phase of the atrial action potential
cards.explanation: The T wave is the voltage change as the ventricles repolarize, and it is broader and lower than the QRS because repolarization spreads more slowly and less uniformly than depolarization. Atrial repolarization is buried within the QRS complex and is not seen separately. Ventricular relaxation is the mechanical event that follows the T wave. The atrial plateau is far too small an event to register at the body surface.

cards.q: What does the PR interval measure?
cards.a: From the start of the P wave to the start of the QRS complex.
options: From the start of the P wave to the start of the QRS complex
From the end of the P wave to the end of the QRS complex
From the start of the P wave to the end of the T wave
From the peak of the P wave to the peak of the R wave
cards.explanation: The PR interval runs from the first sign of atrial depolarization to the first sign of ventricular depolarization, so it contains atrial spread plus the atrioventricular nodal delay, and most of it is the delay. Ending at the end of the QRS would add ventricular depolarization time and no longer isolate conduction from atria to ventricles. Running to the end of the T wave describes something closer to the QT interval plus the PR interval. Intervals are measured from onset to onset, not peak to peak, because the onsets mark when each event starts.

cards.q: What is the normal duration of the PR interval?
cards.a: 0.12 to 0.20 second.
options: 0.02 to 0.06 second
0.12 to 0.20 second
0.25 to 0.35 second
0.40 to 0.50 second
cards.explanation: A normal PR interval is 0.12 to 0.20 second, which is three to five small boxes on standard ECG paper, and most of that time is the atrioventricular nodal delay. A value of 0.02 to 0.06 second would be too short for the atria to depolarize, let alone for the node to hold the impulse. Values above 0.20 second define a first degree block. The 0.40 to 0.50 second range is closer to a normal QT interval.

cards.q: What does the QT interval measure?
cards.a: From the start of the QRS complex to the end of the T wave.
options: From the end of the QRS complex to the start of the T wave
From the start of the P wave to the end of the T wave
From the start of the QRS complex to the end of the T wave
From the peak of the R wave to the peak of the T wave
cards.explanation: The QT interval spans ventricular depolarization and ventricular repolarization together, so it corresponds closely to the duration of the ventricular action potential and to ventricular systole. Measuring from the end of the QRS to the start of the T wave describes the ST segment, which is only the plateau portion. Starting at the P wave would include atrial events and the nodal delay. Peak to peak measurement misses the onset of depolarization and the end of repolarization, which are the boundaries that matter.

cards.q: Why is atrial repolarization not visible as its own wave on a normal ECG?
cards.a: It happens during ventricular depolarization and is buried under the QRS.
options: Atrial repolarization produces no ion movement and therefore no voltage at all
It appears only in the chest leads and never in the limb leads
The atria do not repolarize until the next beat has already begun
It happens during ventricular depolarization and is buried under the QRS
cards.explanation: Atrial repolarization generates a genuine but small signal that happens to coincide with ventricular depolarization, and the ventricular mass is so much larger that the QRS drowns it out. The atria certainly do repolarize within the same beat, otherwise they could not be excited again. Repolarization is K+ efflux and does generate voltage; it is simply overwhelmed. Lead choice does not rescue it, because the timing overlap is the same in every lead.

cards.q: What is the normal duration of the QRS complex?
cards.a: Less than 0.12 second.
options: Less than 0.12 second
0.12 to 0.20 second
0.20 to 0.30 second
0.30 to 0.40 second
cards.explanation: Normal ventricular depolarization is complete in under 0.12 second, usually 0.06 to 0.10 second, because the Purkinje network distributes the impulse almost simultaneously. A QRS of 0.12 to 0.20 second is wide and indicates that activation is spreading through muscle rather than through the fast conducting system. The 0.12 to 0.20 second range is the normal window for the PR interval, not the QRS. Values above 0.20 second are far outside the normal range for ventricular depolarization.

cards.q: Conduction through the atrioventricular node slows. Which ECG measurement lengthens?
cards.a: The PR interval.
options: The QRS duration
The QT interval
The PR interval
The T wave duration
cards.explanation: The PR interval contains the nodal delay, so anything that slows conduction between atria and ventricles stretches it while leaving the rest of the tracing untouched. QRS duration reflects how fast the ventricles depolarize once the impulse arrives, which is a His and Purkinje question, not a nodal one. The QT interval reflects ventricular depolarization and repolarization and is unaffected by how long the impulse waited at the node. The T wave reflects repolarization only.

cards.q: A drug prolongs ventricular repolarization. Which ECG measurement lengthens?
cards.a: The QT interval.
options: The P wave duration
The ST segment only, with no change in QT
The PR interval
The QT interval
cards.explanation: The QT interval covers depolarization through the end of repolarization, so a slower phase 3 pushes the end of the T wave later and lengthens QT. The PR interval measures conduction from atria to ventricles and is unchanged by a repolarization effect. P wave duration reflects atrial depolarization only. The ST segment may shift too, but the point of the QT interval is precisely that it captures repolarization, so it cannot stay constant while repolarization slows.

cards.q: A tracing shows a QRS complex lasting 0.16 second. What does that tell you about ventricular activation?
