cards.a: Part of the ventricle is reached by slow muscle to muscle spread.
options: The atrioventricular node is conducting the impulse too quickly
The ventricles are repolarizing more slowly than they normally would
The ventricles are depolarizing faster than they normally would
Part of the ventricle is reached by slow muscle to muscle spread
cards.explanation: A wide QRS means ventricular depolarization is taking longer than the Purkinje system would allow, which happens when part of the ventricle has to be reached by slow cell to cell conduction through working muscle. A longer QRS is by definition slower activation, not faster. Atrioventricular conduction speed shows up in the PR interval and does not widen the QRS. Repolarization is the T wave and the QT interval, not the QRS.

cards.q: Ventricular muscle mass increases substantially. What would you expect on the ECG?
cards.a: A taller QRS complex, because more muscle is depolarizing at once.
options: A shorter PR interval, because conduction distance is greater
A smaller T wave, because repolarization requires less charge
A taller P wave, because atrial pressure rises
A taller QRS complex, because more muscle is depolarizing at once
cards.explanation: The size of a deflection reflects the amount of tissue depolarizing at that moment, so a thicker ventricular wall generates a larger voltage and a taller QRS. The P wave reflects atrial depolarization, which is not what has changed here. Greater distance would tend to lengthen conduction time, not shorten the PR interval, and the PR interval is dominated by the nodal delay in any case. More muscle repolarizing produces more voltage in the T wave, not less.

cards.q: Which phase of the ventricular action potential does the T wave correspond to?
cards.a: Phase 3, repolarization.
options: Phase 0, the upstroke
Phase 2, the plateau
Phase 3, repolarization
Phase 4, the resting potential
cards.explanation: The T wave is the surface record of ventricular repolarization, which is phase 3, when K+ efflux is no longer balanced by inward Ca2+ current. Phase 0 in millions of cells at once produces the QRS complex. Phase 2 is the plateau, during which the ventricles are uniformly depolarized and the tracing is flat. Phase 4 is the interval between action potentials, which appears as the flat line from the end of the T wave to the next P wave.

cards.q: Why is the segment between the end of the QRS and the start of the T wave normally flat?
cards.a: All ventricular cells sit at the same potential during the plateau.
options: The recording electrodes are electrically disconnected during this period
The atria are repolarizing and cancel the ventricular signal exactly
No ion movement is occurring anywhere in the heart at that moment
All ventricular cells sit at the same potential during the plateau
cards.explanation: Surface electrodes register differences in charge between regions, so when the whole ventricular mass is sitting in the plateau at the same potential there is no difference to detect and the trace stays on the baseline. Plenty of ion movement is happening, since Ca2+ is entering and K+ is leaving in every cell; it is the uniformity that hides it. The electrodes stay connected throughout. Atrial repolarization is much smaller than any ventricular signal and could not cancel one exactly.

cards.q: Why is the QRS complex much larger than the P wave on a normal ECG?
cards.a: The ventricles contain far more muscle mass, so more charge moves at once.
options: The recording electrodes are closer to the ventricles than to the atria
Ventricular depolarization lasts longer, which raises the recorded amplitude
Ventricular cells depolarize to a more positive peak voltage than atrial cells
The ventricles contain far more muscle mass, so more charge moves at once
cards.explanation: Deflection size on an ECG tracks the total amount of tissue changing charge at that moment, and the ventricular walls contain several times the muscle of the atria. Peak membrane voltage in a single cell is similar in the two chambers, so that is not the source of the difference. Electrode distance plays a small role in individual leads but does not explain the consistent size difference across leads. Duration and amplitude are separate measurements, and ventricular depolarization is actually quite brief.

cards.q: An ECG shows a PR interval of 0.16 second, a QRS duration of 0.08 second, and a QT interval of 0.36 second at a rate of 75 beats per minute. What do these measurements indicate?
cards.a: All three intervals are within normal limits.
options: The PR interval is prolonged beyond normal
The QRS complex is abnormally wide
The QT interval is prolonged for this rate
All three intervals are within normal limits
cards.explanation: A PR interval of 0.12 to 0.20 second, a QRS under 0.12 second, and a QT near 0.36 to 0.44 second at a normal rate are all ordinary values, so this tracing shows normal conduction and normal repolarization. Prolonged PR means greater than 0.20 second, which 0.16 is not. A wide QRS means 0.12 second or more, and 0.08 is comfortably below that. A QT of 0.36 second at 75 beats per minute is normal, since QT shortens as rate rises.

cards.q: A tracing at 60 beats per minute shows a normal P wave, a QRS of 0.09 second, and a QT interval of 0.60 second. Which cellular change best explains it?
cards.a: Reduced K+ efflux during phase 3, which prolongs repolarization.
options: Reduced K+ efflux during phase 3, which prolongs repolarization
Reduced Na+ influx during phase 0, which slows the upstroke
Slower conduction through the atrioventricular node
Increased K+ leak conductance at rest, which deepens the resting potential
cards.explanation: The QT interval is long while the QRS is normal, so depolarization is fine and the delay is in repolarization, which depends on outward K+ current during phase 3. Slower Na+ entry during phase 0 would widen the QRS, which this tracing does not show. Slowed nodal conduction would lengthen the PR interval instead. More resting K+ conductance would make the resting potential more negative but would if anything speed repolarization, not delay it.

cards.q: A strip shows regular P waves and regular QRS complexes, but the distance from each P wave to the next QRS keeps changing. Which measurement cannot be meaningfully reported?
cards.a: The PR interval, because the P waves and QRS are unrelated.
options: The QT interval, because the T waves belong to different beats
The P wave duration, because the atria are not depolarizing normally
The QRS duration, because the complexes are irregular in shape
The PR interval, because the P waves and QRS are unrelated
cards.explanation: A PR interval only means something when the same impulse produces the P wave and then the QRS, so when the two are marching at independent rates there is no interval to measure, only a changing coincidence. QRS duration is measured within a single complex and is perfectly reportable here, since each complex is itself regular. The QT interval is also measured within one ventricular beat, from that beat's QRS to that beat's T wave. The P waves are regular and normal in this description, so their duration can be measured too.

cards.q: At a heart rate of 60 beats per minute the QT interval is 0.40 second. What fraction of each cardiac cycle are the ventricles electrically active, and what does the rest of the cycle represent?
cards.a: About 40 percent, with the remainder representing electrical diastole between beats.
options: About 60 percent, with the remainder representing atrial depolarization
About 40 percent, with the remainder representing the plateau phase
About 25 percent, with the remainder representing the atrioventricular delay
About 40 percent, with the remainder representing electrical diastole between beats
cards.explanation: At 60 beats per minute each cycle lasts 1.00 second, so a QT interval of 0.40 second occupies 40 percent of it, and the remaining 0.60 second is the time from the end of the T wave to the next QRS, when the ventricles are repolarized and refilling. The atrioventricular delay is roughly 0.10 second and accounts for only a small slice of the remainder. Atrial depolarization is the brief P wave, not the majority of the cycle. The plateau is contained inside the QT interval, so it cannot be the remainder.

cards.q: On standard ECG paper, how much time does one small box represent?
cards.a: 0.04 second.
options: 0.01 second
0.04 second
0.10 second
0.20 second
cards.explanation: Standard paper runs at 25 mm per second and each small box is 1 mm wide, so one small box is 1 divided by 25, which is 0.04 second. A value of 0.20 second is the large box, made of five small ones. A value of 0.10 second would not divide evenly into the grid at standard paper speed. A hundredth of a second is finer than the grid can resolve.

cards.q: How much time does one large box represent on standard ECG paper?
cards.a: 0.20 second.
options: 0.04 second
0.10 second
0.20 second
0.50 second
cards.explanation: A large box contains five small boxes, and five times 0.04 second is 0.20 second, which is why five large boxes make one full second. The 0.04 second value belongs to a single small box. Neither 0.10 nor 0.50 second corresponds to any square on the standard grid, and using either would throw off every rate calculation.

cards.q: Which rule gives heart rate from the number of small boxes between two R waves?
cards.a: Divide 1500 by the number of small boxes.
options: Divide 1500 by the number of small boxes
Divide 300 by the number of small boxes
Multiply the number of small boxes by 10
Divide 60 by the number of small boxes
cards.explanation: There are 1500 small boxes in a minute, since each is 0.04 second and 60 divided by 0.04 is 1500, so dividing 1500 by the boxes between beats gives beats per minute. Dividing 300 is the rule for large boxes, and using it on small boxes underestimates the rate fivefold. Multiplying by 10 is the six second strip rule applied to QRS complexes, not to boxes. Dividing 60 by boxes would only work if each box were a full second.

cards.q: How do you estimate heart rate from a six second rhythm strip?
cards.a: Count the QRS complexes in the strip and multiply by 10.
options: Count the small boxes in the strip and divide by 6
Count the P waves in the strip and multiply by 4
Count the QRS complexes and multiply by 6, since the strip is 6 seconds
Count the QRS complexes in the strip and multiply by 10
cards.explanation: Six seconds is one tenth of a minute, so the number of beats in that window multiplied by 10 gives beats per minute, and this method works even when the rhythm is irregular. Multiplying by 6 would treat the strip as ten seconds long. Counting boxes and dividing by 6 measures time rather than rate. Counting P waves gives the atrial rate, which equals the ventricular rate only when every P wave is conducted.

cards.q: Which findings define normal sinus rhythm?
cards.a: An upright P before every QRS, a constant PR, and a rate of 60 to 100.
options: An upright P before every QRS, a constant PR, and a rate of 60 to 100
A P wave after every QRS, a constant PR interval, and a rate of 60 to 100 beats per minute
An upright P wave before every QRS, a variable PR interval, and any rate
No visible P waves, a narrow QRS, and a rate of 60 to 100 beats per minute
cards.explanation: Sinus rhythm means the sinoatrial node started each beat and the impulse followed the normal path, which shows up as an upright P wave preceding every QRS, a PR interval that is the same on every beat, and a rate in the normal range. A P wave following the QRS would mean the atria were activated after the ventricles, so the beat did not begin in the sinoatrial node. A PR interval that varies from beat to beat means the P waves and QRS complexes are not linked. Absent P waves mean the atria are not depolarizing in an organized way.

cards.q: At what heart rate does bradycardia begin?
cards.a: Below 60 beats per minute.
options: Below 100 beats per minute
Below 80 beats per minute
Below 60 beats per minute
Below 40 beats per minute
cards.explanation: Bradycardia is a resting rate under 60 beats per minute, the lower edge of the normal 60 to 100 range, and tachycardia is a rate above 100. A cutoff of 100 would label most normal resting hearts as slow. A cutoff of 80 sits in the middle of the normal range. A cutoff of 40 would miss the many rates between 40 and 60 that are genuinely below normal, although rates that low are usually a junctional or ventricular escape rhythm.

cards.q: What defines a first degree heart block on an ECG?
cards.a: A PR interval longer than 0.20 second, with a QRS following every P wave.
options: A PR interval longer than 0.20 second, with a QRS following every P wave
A PR interval longer than 0.20 second, with occasional P waves not followed by a QRS
P waves and QRS complexes at completely independent rates
A QRS complex wider than 0.12 second with a normal PR interval
cards.explanation: In a first degree block every impulse still reaches the ventricles, it just takes too long crossing the atrioventricular node, so the PR interval is stretched beyond 0.20 second but each P wave is still followed by its own QRS. Dropped beats, where some P waves are not conducted, describe a second degree block. Complete independence of P waves and QRS complexes is third degree, or complete, block. A wide QRS is a problem in the ventricular conduction system, not at the node.

cards.q: What defines a complete heart block on an ECG?
cards.a: P waves and QRS complexes occur regularly but at independent rates.
options: P waves are absent and the QRS complexes are irregular in timing
The PR interval lengthens progressively until a QRS is dropped
P waves and QRS complexes occur regularly but at independent rates
Every P wave is followed by a QRS, but the PR interval exceeds 0.20 second
cards.explanation: In complete block nothing crosses from atria to ventricles, so the sinoatrial node keeps pacing the atria at its own rate while an escape pacemaker below the block paces the ventricles at a slower rate, and the two are unrelated. P waves are present and regular in complete block; they are simply not conducted. A progressively lengthening PR interval before a dropped beat is one form of second degree block. A long but constant PR interval with every beat conducted is first degree block.

cards.q: An ECG shows 20 small boxes between consecutive R waves. What is the heart rate?
cards.a: 75 beats per minute.
options: 15 beats per minute
60 beats per minute
75 beats per minute
100 beats per minute
cards.explanation: Dividing 1500 by 20 small boxes gives 75 beats per minute, and you can check it the long way: 20 boxes times 0.04 second is 0.80 second per beat, and 60 divided by 0.80 is 75. The value of 15 comes from applying the large box rule of 300 divided by boxes to small boxes instead. A rate of 60 would require 25 small boxes between beats. A rate of 100 would require 15 small boxes.

cards.q: An ECG shows exactly 5 large boxes between consecutive R waves. What is the heart rate?
cards.a: 60 beats per minute.
options: 50 beats per minute
60 beats per minute
75 beats per minute
300 beats per minute
cards.explanation: Dividing 300 by 5 large boxes gives 60 beats per minute, which makes sense because five large boxes is exactly one second. A rate of 75 would correspond to 4 large boxes. A rate of 50 would correspond to 6 large boxes. The figure of 300 is the rate for a single large box between beats, which would be an extraordinarily fast rhythm.

cards.q: A six second rhythm strip contains 13 QRS complexes. What is the rate, and how is it classified?
cards.a: 130 beats per minute, which is tachycardia.
options: 130 beats per minute, which is normal
13 beats per minute, which is bradycardia
78 beats per minute, which is normal
130 beats per minute, which is tachycardia
cards.explanation: Six seconds is a tenth of a minute, so 13 complexes times 10 gives 130 beats per minute, which is above the normal ceiling of 100 and therefore tachycardia. Multiplying by 6 instead of 10 gives 78 and treats the strip as ten seconds long. A rate of 130 cannot be called normal, since the normal range stops at 100. Reporting 13 forgets to scale the six second window up to a full minute.

cards.q: The interval between R waves on a strip is 1.2 seconds. What is the rate, and how is it classified?
cards.a: 50 beats per minute, which is bradycardia.
options: 50 beats per minute, which is bradycardia
72 beats per minute, which is normal
50 beats per minute, which is normal
120 beats per minute, which is tachycardia
cards.explanation: Rate is 60 seconds divided by the cycle length, and 60 divided by 1.2 is 50 beats per minute, which falls below 60 and is therefore bradycardia. A rate of 72 would mean a cycle length of about 0.83 second. Calling 50 normal ignores the lower limit of the normal range. The figure of 120 comes from treating 1.2 as if it were the rate rather than the interval.

cards.q: A strip shows an upright P wave before every QRS complex, a PR interval of 0.24 second that is identical on every beat, and a rate of 68 beats per minute. How is this classified?
cards.a: Sinus rhythm with a first degree heart block.
options: Normal sinus rhythm with normal conduction
Sinus bradycardia with an otherwise normal tracing
Sinus rhythm with a first degree heart block
Complete heart block with an escape rhythm
cards.explanation: Every P wave is conducted and the rate is normal, so the rhythm is sinus, but a PR interval of 0.24 second is longer than the 0.20 second limit, which means the impulse is being held too long at the atrioventricular node. Normal sinus rhythm would require a PR interval of 0.20 second or less. Sinus bradycardia would require a rate below 60, and 68 is within range. Complete block would show P waves and QRS complexes at unrelated rates rather than a fixed PR interval on every beat.

cards.q: A strip shows P waves marching along at 82 per minute and QRS complexes at 34 per minute, with no consistent relationship between them. How is this classified?
cards.a: Complete heart block.
options: Sinus bradycardia
First degree heart block
Complete heart block
Normal sinus rhythm with a slow ventricular response
cards.explanation: Two independent rates with no fixed PR interval means no impulse is crossing from atria to ventricles, so the sinoatrial node is pacing the atria while an escape pacemaker below the block drives the ventricles at 34 per minute. Sinus bradycardia would show a single slow rate with a P wave before each QRS. A first degree block still conducts every beat, so atrial and ventricular rates would be identical. Sinus rhythm by definition requires each QRS to be produced by the preceding P wave.

cards.q: A strip shows a rate of 96 beats per minute, an upright P wave before every QRS, and a constant PR interval of 0.16 second. How is this classified?
cards.a: Normal sinus rhythm.
options: First degree heart block
Sinus bradycardia
Sinus tachycardia
Normal sinus rhythm
cards.explanation: All three criteria are met: the beat starts in the sinoatrial node as shown by the upright P wave, conduction is normal as shown by the constant PR interval within 0.12 to 0.20 second, and 96 falls inside the normal range of 60 to 100. Tachycardia would require a rate above 100, and 96 is close but still under the limit. A first degree block would require a PR interval longer than 0.20 second. Bradycardia would require a rate below 60.

cards.q: On a strip the P waves are 15 small boxes apart and the R waves are 50 small boxes apart, and no fixed relationship exists between them. State the atrial rate, the ventricular rate, and the rhythm.
cards.a: Atrial rate 100, ventricular rate 30, complete heart block.
options: Atrial rate 100, ventricular rate 30, complete heart block
Atrial rate 100, ventricular rate 50, first degree heart block
Atrial rate 30, ventricular rate 100, complete heart block
Atrial rate 60, ventricular rate 30, sinus bradycardia
cards.explanation: Using 1500 divided by small boxes, the atria are firing at 1500 divided by 15, which is 100 per minute, and the ventricles at 1500 divided by 50, which is 30 per minute, and because the two are unrelated the rhythm is complete block with a slow ventricular escape. A ventricular rate of 50 would require 30 small boxes between R waves. Swapping the two rates ignores that the closer spaced waves must be the faster rhythm. Sinus bradycardia requires every P wave to conduct, which cannot be true when the rates differ.

cards.q: A strip shows 25 small boxes between R waves, an upright P wave before every QRS, and a PR interval of 0.32 second on every beat. State the rate and the rhythm.
cards.a: 60 beats per minute, sinus rhythm with a first degree heart block.
options: 75 beats per minute, sinus rhythm with a first degree heart block
48 beats per minute, sinus bradycardia with a complete heart block
60 beats per minute, normal sinus rhythm
60 beats per minute, sinus rhythm with a first degree heart block
cards.explanation: Dividing 1500 by 25 small boxes gives 60 beats per minute, which is the bottom of the normal range and not bradycardia, and the PR interval of 0.32 second is well beyond the 0.20 second limit, so this is sinus rhythm with a first degree block. Calling it normal ignores the prolonged PR interval. A rate of 75 would require 20 small boxes between R waves. A complete block cannot have a fixed PR interval on every beat, and 48 does not follow from 25 small boxes.

cards.q: A patient's atria are depolarizing at 75 per minute but the ventricles are contracting at 35 per minute, independently. Which tissue is driving the ventricles, and why is the rate so low?
cards.a: A His and Purkinje escape pacemaker, firing at only 20 to 40 per minute.
options: The atrioventricular node above the block, pacing at 40 to 60 per minute
Ventricular muscle itself, which depolarizes spontaneously when stretched
The sinoatrial node, conducting through a slow accessory pathway
A His and Purkinje escape pacemaker, firing at only 20 to 40 per minute
cards.explanation: When no impulse crosses from the atria, the fastest pacemaker below the block takes over, and ventricular conducting tissue drifts to threshold only 20 to 40 times a minute, which fits the observed 35. If the sinoatrial impulse were reaching the ventricles by any route, the two rates would be linked rather than independent. A junctional escape above the block cannot drive the ventricles, since the block lies between it and the ventricular muscle, and it would also give a faster rate of 40 to 60. Ordinary ventricular muscle has a stable resting potential and no pacemaker current, so it cannot generate a rhythm.

cards.q: On a strip the R to R interval varies between 20 and 25 small boxes, and each QRS is preceded by an upright P wave with a constant PR interval. What is the range of the heart rate, and does this meet the definition of tachycardia?
cards.a: About 60 to 75 beats per minute, which is not tachycardia.
options: About 60 to 75 beats per minute, which is not tachycardia
About 60 to 75 beats per minute, which is tachycardia because the rhythm varies
About 75 to 100 beats per minute, which is not tachycardia
About 100 to 125 beats per minute, which is tachycardia
cards.explanation: Dividing 1500 by 25 gives 60 and dividing 1500 by 20 gives 75, so the rate swings between 60 and 75, entirely inside the normal range. Tachycardia is defined by rate alone, above 100 beats per minute, so variation in the interval does not make a rhythm fast. A range of 75 to 100 would require intervals of 15 to 20 small boxes. A range of 100 to 125 would require intervals of 12 to 15 small boxes.

cards.q: In a lead II recording, which electrodes serve as the negative and positive poles?
cards.a: Right arm negative, left leg positive.
options: Left leg negative, left arm positive
Right leg negative, right arm positive
Left arm negative, right arm positive
Right arm negative, left leg positive
cards.explanation: Lead II runs from the right arm as the negative pole to the left leg as the positive pole, which points down and to the left, roughly along the path the impulse travels through the heart. Left arm negative with right arm positive is a reversed version of lead I. Left leg negative with left arm positive reverses lead III. The right leg electrode is a ground reference and is not one of the recording poles in the standard limb leads.

cards.q: How fast does ECG paper run during a standard recording?
cards.a: 25 mm per second.
options: 5 mm per second
25 mm per second
50 mm per second
100 mm per second
cards.explanation: Standard paper speed is 25 mm per second, which is what makes each 1 mm small box equal 0.04 second and each 5 mm large box equal 0.20 second. At 50 mm per second every interval would appear twice as wide and every measured duration would be doubled if you used the standard box values. Speeds of 5 or 100 mm per second are not clinical standards and would make the usual box rules meaningless.

cards.q: What is the standard vertical calibration of an ECG recording?
cards.a: 10 mm equals 1 mV.
options: 1 mm equals 1 mV
10 mm equals 1 mV
10 mm equals 10 mV
25 mm equals 1 mV
cards.explanation: Standard calibration makes 10 mm of vertical deflection equal 1 mV, which is why a calibration pulse two large boxes tall appears at the start of a proper recording. If 1 mm equalled 1 mV, every normal QRS would run off the paper. Ten millimeters for 10 mV would flatten normal complexes into near invisibility. The 25 mm figure belongs to the horizontal axis, as paper speed, not the vertical one.

cards.q: Why is lead II usually chosen for a rhythm strip?
cards.a: Its axis lies along the path the impulse takes, so waves are upright.
options: It records from the sinoatrial node directly, unlike the other limb leads
It is the only lead that is unaffected by skeletal muscle artifact
It is the only limb lead that records atrial activity at all
Its axis lies along the path the impulse takes, so waves are upright
cards.explanation: Depolarization normally travels from the upper right toward the lower left of the heart, and lead II looks along that same direction, so it produces the clearest upright P wave and the largest QRS, which makes counting and measuring easy. Every limb lead records atrial activity; lead II just shows it best. No surface lead records from the sinoatrial node itself, which is far too small to generate a surface signal. Muscle artifact contaminates any lead if the subject moves or tenses.

cards.q: Which mechanical event follows the P wave?
cards.a: Atrial contraction.
options: Atrial contraction
Ventricular contraction
Closure of the semilunar valves
Ventricular filling by passive flow
cards.explanation: The P wave is atrial depolarization, and the atria contract a few tens of milliseconds later, once Ca2+ has reached the myofilaments. Ventricular contraction follows the QRS, not the P wave, and is separated from atrial contraction by the atrioventricular nodal delay. The semilunar valves close at the end of ventricular ejection, near the end of the T wave. Passive filling happens throughout diastole, before the P wave rather than because of it.

cards.q: Which mechanical event follows the QRS complex?
cards.a: Ventricular contraction, with closure of the atrioventricular valves.
options: Atrial contraction, with opening of the atrioventricular valves
Ventricular relaxation, with opening of the atrioventricular valves
Ventricular contraction, with closure of the atrioventricular valves
Atrial relaxation, with closure of the semilunar valves
cards.explanation: The QRS records ventricular depolarization, and contraction follows within a few tens of milliseconds, raising ventricular pressure above atrial pressure and slamming the atrioventricular valves shut, which produces the first heart sound. Atrial contraction follows the P wave, which comes earlier in the cycle. Ventricular relaxation follows the T wave. The semilunar valves close at the end of ejection rather than at its beginning.

cards.q: Which mechanical event follows the T wave?
cards.a: Ventricular relaxation, with closure of the semilunar valves.
options: Ventricular relaxation, with closure of the semilunar valves
Ventricular contraction, with closure of the atrioventricular valves
Atrial contraction, with a rise in atrial pressure
Isovolumetric contraction of the ventricles
cards.explanation: The T wave is ventricular repolarization, and relaxation follows it, ventricular pressure falls below aortic and pulmonary pressure, the semilunar valves snap shut and produce the second heart sound. Ventricular contraction and atrioventricular valve closure follow the QRS, at the other end of ventricular systole. Atrial contraction follows the P wave. Isovolumetric contraction happens immediately after the QRS, at the start of systole, not after the T wave.

cards.q: Why is conductive gel applied under an ECG electrode?
cards.a: It lowers the electrical resistance between the skin and the electrode.
options: It prevents current from the recorder from reaching the subject's skin
It blocks skeletal muscle signals while allowing cardiac signals through
It amplifies the cardiac signal before it reaches the recorder input
It lowers the electrical resistance between the skin and the electrode
cards.explanation: Dry skin is a poor conductor, and the voltages reaching the surface are only about a millivolt, so gel lowers the impedance at the contact and stops the signal from being lost in noise. Amplification is done by the recorder, not by the gel. An ECG only records, so no current is being sent into the subject that needs blocking. Gel cannot distinguish one tissue's signals from another's; muscle artifact is reduced by having the subject relax, not by the gel.

cards.q: On your subject's lead II strip, the PR interval measures 4 small boxes. What is its duration and is it normal?
cards.a: 0.16 second, which is normal.
options: 0.16 second, which is prolonged
0.04 second, which is normal
0.40 second, which is prolonged
0.16 second, which is normal
cards.explanation: Four small boxes at 0.04 second each is 0.16 second, comfortably inside the normal PR range of 0.12 to 0.20 second. Calling 0.16 second prolonged applies the wrong cutoff, since prolongation begins above 0.20 second. Reporting 0.04 second uses the value of a single box instead of four. Reporting 0.40 second multiplies by 0.10 second per box, which is not the standard grid value.

cards.q: You measure a QRS complex spanning 2 small boxes. What is its duration and what does it tell you?
cards.a: 0.08 second, indicating normal ventricular conduction.
options: 0.08 second, indicating that ventricular activation is abnormally slow
0.20 second, indicating a bundle branch block is present
0.02 second, indicating an unusually fast ventricular rate
0.08 second, indicating normal ventricular conduction
cards.explanation: Two small boxes is 0.08 second, which is under the 0.12 second ceiling, so the impulse is reaching the ventricular muscle through the fast bundle branch and Purkinje network as it should. A duration under the normal limit cannot indicate slow activation. Reading 2 boxes as 0.20 second uses 0.10 second per box, which is not the standard grid value. QRS duration measures how long ventricular depolarization takes, not how often it happens, so it says nothing about rate.

cards.q: You measure the QT interval as 9 small boxes. What is its duration?
cards.a: 0.36 second.
options: 0.09 second
0.18 second
0.36 second
0.45 second
cards.explanation: Nine small boxes at 0.04 second each is 0.36 second, a normal QT interval at an ordinary resting rate. Reporting 0.09 second treats each box as 0.01 second. Reporting 0.18 second uses 0.02 second per box. Reporting 0.45 second uses 0.05 second per box, which is close to the correct value but not the standard grid.

cards.q: During a simultaneous ECG and heart sound recording, when does the first heart sound occur?
cards.a: Just after the QRS complex, as the atrioventricular valves close.
options: At the peak of the T wave, as the ventricles begin to relax
Midway between the T wave and the next P wave
Just after the P wave, as the atria begin to contract
Just after the QRS complex, as the atrioventricular valves close
cards.explanation: The first heart sound is the atrioventricular valves closing, which happens as soon as ventricular pressure rises above atrial pressure, a few tens of milliseconds after the QRS depolarizes the ventricles. Atrial contraction after the P wave is quiet in a healthy heart. Valve closure at the end of the T wave produces the second heart sound, not the first. The gap between the T wave and the next P wave is diastole, when both valve sets are quiet.

cards.q: On the same recording, when does the second heart sound occur?
cards.a: At the end of the T wave, as the semilunar valves close.
options: At the start of the QRS complex, as the ventricles depolarize
In the middle of the PR interval, as the impulse crosses the atrioventricular node
At the end of the T wave, as the semilunar valves close
Just before the P wave, as the ventricles finish filling
cards.explanation: The second heart sound is aortic and pulmonary valve closure, which happens when ventricular pressure falls below arterial pressure at the end of ejection, and that coincides closely with the end of the T wave. The QRS marks the start of ventricular systole, which is where the first heart sound belongs. Nodal conduction during the PR interval is silent, both electrically at the surface and mechanically. The interval before the P wave is late diastole, when the ventricles are filling quietly.

cards.q: Your subject's recording shows a fuzzy, high frequency baseline that disappears when the subject stops talking and relaxes the arms. What is the source?
cards.a: Electrical activity from nearby skeletal muscle.
options: Depolarization of the atrioventricular node reaching the surface
Repolarization of the atria becoming visible in this lead
A paper speed that has been set too high for the recording
Electrical activity from nearby skeletal muscle
cards.explanation: Skeletal muscle generates its own action potentials, and any contracting muscle near an electrode adds a rapid irregular signal on top of the cardiac trace, which is why subjects are asked to lie still and relax. The atrioventricular node is far too small to produce any surface signal at all. Atrial repolarization is a slow low amplitude event hidden inside the QRS, not a source of high frequency noise. Changing paper speed stretches or compresses the trace horizontally but does not add noise.

cards.q: Why does each wave of the ECG come slightly before the mechanical event it is associated with?
cards.a: Excitation contraction coupling takes time before force develops.
options: The mechanical event begins first and the electrode records it afterward
The recorder introduces a fixed electronic delay in the mechanical channel
Excitation contraction coupling takes time before force develops
Blood must move through the chambers before the signal reaches the skin
cards.explanation: Excitation contraction coupling has real steps: the action potential opens L-type Ca2+ channels, that Ca2+ triggers release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, Ca2+ binds troponin, and only then do cross bridges generate force, so contraction always lags depolarization by a few tens of milliseconds. The delay is physiological, not an artifact of the recording equipment. The electrical signal reaches the skin almost instantly, well before blood has moved anywhere. Reversing the order would mean muscle contracts before it is excited, which does not happen in cardiac muscle.

cards.q: On your strip, the interval from the start of the QRS to the end of the T wave measures 10 small boxes. State the duration and what is happening mechanically at the end of that interval.
cards.a: 0.40 second, and the ventricles are beginning to relax as the semilunar valves close.
options: 0.40 second, and the ventricles are beginning to contract as the atrioventricular valves close
0.10 second, and the atria are contracting to complete ventricular filling
1.00 second, and the next beat is beginning at the sinoatrial node
0.40 second, and the ventricles are beginning to relax as the semilunar valves close
cards.explanation: Ten small boxes at 0.04 second each is 0.40 second, and that interval, the QT, covers ventricular depolarization through the end of repolarization, so its end marks the point where the ventricles stop generating force, pressure falls, and the semilunar valves close. Contraction and atrioventricular valve closure happen at the beginning of the interval, right after the QRS. Atrial contraction belongs to the P wave, well before the QRS. Reporting 1.00 second would require 25 small boxes.

cards.q: You record a subject at rest and again immediately after exercise. The heart rate rises from 60 to 150 beats per minute. Which part of the cardiac cycle shortens the most, and what is the consequence for the ventricles?
cards.a: Diastole shortens the most, so there is much less time for ventricular filling.
options: The PR interval shortens the most, so atrial contraction is lost
The QRS shortens the most, so ventricular activation becomes uneven
Diastole shortens the most, so there is much less time for ventricular filling
Systole shortens the most, so there is less time for ejection
cards.explanation: Going from 60 to 150 beats per minute cuts the cycle from 1.00 second to 0.40 second, and because systole is defended and shortens only modestly, nearly all of the lost time comes out of diastole, which squeezes filling time and makes the atrial contribution to filling matter far more. Systole does shorten a little as the action potential shortens, but it is not where most of the time is lost. The PR interval does shorten with sympathetic drive, but by hundredths of a second, and atrial contraction is not lost. QRS duration is set by conduction speed through the Purkinje system and barely changes with rate.

cards.q: A lead II recording shows a P wave, QRS complex, and T wave that are all inverted, with normal intervals and a normal rate. What is the most likely explanation?
cards.a: The right arm and left leg electrodes have been reversed.
options: The paper speed was set to 50 mm per second instead of 25
The gain was set to 20 mm per millivolt instead of 10
The subject has a complete heart block with dissociated beats
The right arm and left leg electrodes have been reversed
cards.explanation: Every deflection is upside down while the timing and the rate are untouched, which points to a polarity problem rather than a cardiac one: swapping the negative right arm electrode with the positive left leg electrode reverses the recording axis and flips the whole complex. A complete heart block would disturb the relationship between P waves and QRS complexes, not simply invert them. A faster paper speed stretches the trace horizontally without flipping anything. Doubling the gain makes deflections taller, still in the same direction.

cards.q: Your subject's strip shows an upright P wave, then a QRS, then a T wave. Put the following in the order they actually occur in one beat: closure of the atrioventricular valves, atrial contraction, ventricular repolarization, ventricular depolarization.
cards.a: Atrial contraction, ventricular depolarization, closure of the atrioventricular valves, ventricular repolarization.
options: Ventricular depolarization, atrial contraction, closure of the atrioventricular valves, ventricular repolarization
Atrial contraction, closure of the atrioventricular valves, ventricular depolarization, ventricular repolarization
Atrial contraction, ventricular depolarization, closure of the atrioventricular valves, ventricular repolarization
Closure of the atrioventricular valves, atrial contraction, ventricular depolarization, ventricular repolarization
cards.explanation: The P wave comes first and atrial contraction follows it, then the QRS marks ventricular depolarization, then contraction raises ventricular pressure above atrial pressure and shuts the atrioventricular valves, and finally the T wave records repolarization. Putting ventricular depolarization before atrial contraction reverses the order the conduction system imposes. Closing the atrioventricular valves before ventricular depolarization is impossible, since the pressure that closes them is generated by the contraction that depolarization triggers. Valve closure certainly cannot precede atrial contraction, which occurs while those valves are still open and blood is flowing through them.
